Which features, which encoding? Compact feature spaces for quantum classification of myocardial infarction on PTB-XL

1. Dataset and cohort

The cohort is 14,965 PTB-XL recordings: 5,454 with myocardial infarction (MI) and 9,511 normal (NORM). They come from 13,436 patients. The feature table and the metadata file were matched on ecg_id before any modelling.

2. Candidate feature pool

All features were extracted upstream (Pan–Tompkins R-peak detection, J-point at the S-wave nadir + 20 ms, baseline from the PR segment). The pool is every numeric column other than identifiers and labels: 251 candidates with age and sex, and 249 ECG-only candidates. The quantum runs use the ECG-only pool, so results can be attributed to the ECG alone.

GroupCountExamples
Demographic / recording3age, sex, number of beats detected
Global ST summaries4max ST elevation / depression, numbers of leads elevated / depressed
Reciprocal-change flags4inferior, anterior, lateral, any
ST morphology (12 leads × 12)144ST amplitude, deviation, slope, area, mean, extrema, variance, curvature
QRS and T wave (12 leads × 8)96R and S amplitude, RS ratio, Q depth and duration, T amplitude, T inversion

3. Splitting and leakage control

  • Every split is grouped by patient_id, so no patient is in more than one of train, validation and test. Patient-grouped, class-stratified 5-fold cross-validation; inside each training set about one eighth is held out for validation.
  • Imputation, standardisation, PCA/PLS, Cohen's d, the correlation filter, mutual information, L1 paths and all selector tuning are fitted on training data only.
  • The 128 patients with both MI and normal recordings stay together in one fold (primary policy); other policies were tested classically and did not change the conclusions.
  • The test fold is scored once and never used for any choice. Metric: test AUC, mean over folds.

4. Feature selectors

Each selector produces a ranked list, so sets for different k are nested. The quantum runs use these:

SelectorIdea
l1Order in which features enter an L1-logistic model as the penalty relaxes
miMutual information with the label, with a |r| < 0.80 redundancy filter
qsepQuantum-aware: separability of the two classes after a single-qubit Ry encoding
cohen_dedupAbsolute Cohen's d, skipping features with |r| ≥ 0.80 to one already chosen
consensus (untuned)Stability screen, then rank consensus of L1, MI and qsep
tuned hybrid (consensus_tuned)Weights over L1, MI and qsep chosen on validation data (successive halving). Tuned at k = 8, then reused at other k. Weights were mostly qsep 0.50–0.75, L1 0–0.50, MI 0–0.25.
pca, plsMix all features into new components (not interpretable)
randomNull baseline

5. The quantum model

  • Circuit: variational quantum classifier (VQC), 8 or 12 qubits, 4 layers (8 layers tested). Each layer is an Ry and an Rz rotation per qubit followed by a ring of CNOT gates. Exactly simulated; nothing was run on a real device.
  • Encoding: angle encoding, angle = π·tanh(z), one feature per qubit per layer. Features beyond the qubit count are loaded in extra rounds (data re-uploading), so k must be a multiple of the qubit count and at most qubits × layers.
  • Read-out: linear. 81 trainable parameters at 8 qubits and 121 at 12 qubits.
  • Training: parameter-shift gradients (batched on GPU), Adam, learning rate 0.01, 300 steps, class-weighted cross-entropy.
  • Cost: 12 qubits is roughly 20–35 times slower than 8 qubits per training (estimated). 16 qubits is not practical with parameter-shift.

6. Classical models and controls

Every quantum result is read against logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF) and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) on the same features and folds, plus the random selector as the null baseline. A parameter-matched size sweep of the MLP (2 to 128 hidden units) tests whether the gap comes from model size.

7. Findings from the classical screen

All values are test AUC, mean of 5 patient-grouped folds.

ModelBest configurationAUCAll 251 features
Random forestcohen_dedup, k = 1280.9680.967
Parameter-matched MLPl1, k = 640.9640.956
Logistic regressionl1, k = 1280.9570.956
  • The data are very separable classically: the ceiling is about 0.97 (RF) and 0.96 (LR, MLP).
  • Feature selection matters only when k is small. At k = 8 the best selector beats random by 0.08 (RF, MLP) to 0.13 (LR); by k = 128 the gap is 0.01 or less.
  • No selector wins everywhere. Age and sex add little (about +0.002 AUC).
This is why the quantum comparison sits at k ≤ 32: it is the range where choosing features can change the result, and where a small circuit can operate at all.

8. Findings from the quantum experiments

8.1 Abstract tier (8 qubits, 4 layers): angle encoding

Angle encoding of 8 selected features reaches AUC about 0.90. Loading more features did not help. Amplitude encoding of all 249 features (0.852) is below angle encoding of 8 well-chosen features.

Selectork = 8k = 16k = 32

old hybrid (PCA + Cohen's d)0.8570.6980.628
random0.7990.6790.606
tuned hybrid0.9050.8650.736
  • Selected features add about +0.10 AUC over random at k = 8.
  • At k = 16 and 32 the earlier selectors were not significantly better than random after correction (fold SD 0.04–0.07).

8.2 Fixed qubit budget: the tuned hybrid keeps the most information

With a fixed number of qubits we loaded more features than the first round (8 qubits: 8 → 16 features; 12 qubits: 12 → 24).

CircuitSelectorFirst roundMore featuresDrop
8 qubitsTuned hybrid0.9050.865−0.04
8 qubitsL10.9000.819−0.08
8 qubitsqsep0.9010.788−0.11
8 qubitsMI0.8920.808−0.08
12 qubitsTuned hybrid0.9120.887−0.025
12 qubitsqsep0.9150.837−0.078

The tuned hybrid is the only selector that holds most of its information when features outnumber qubits; single selectors lose 2–3 times more.

Caveat. The hybrid's edge depends on how features are loaded. It helps when features are loaded in extra rounds, ties when only one round is used, loses to L1 at 32 features on 8 qubits, and ties L1 at 16 features with 8 layers. Weights were tuned at 8 features only.

8.3 More qubits help; more layers do not

  • 12 qubits with 24 features (0.887) beat 8 qubits with 16 features (0.865) and 32 features (0.736).
  • 8 layers gave +0.01 at 8 features and collapsed to 0.57 at 32 features. Confirmed at both 8 and 12 qubits.

8.4 Shuffle control: the circuit uses later-loaded features poorly

Scrambling the later-loaded features costs only about 0.05–0.11 AUC (L1: 0.819 → 0.741 at k = 16, 0.774 → 0.661 at 32; qsep: 0.788 → 0.734, 0.668 → 0.547). Later rounds interfere with earlier ones, so the circuit cannot fully use extra features.

8.5 Mixing features (PCA / PLS) is worse than selecting

At 8 features PLS scored 0.880 and PCA 0.832, below selection (0.89–0.905). At 16 and 32 features both fell to about 0.50 (chance). The 16 and 32 values are approximate and must be checked against the result tables before quoting.

The VQC L1 values are 0.911 and 0.837 in the data; earlier notes had 0.914 and 0.838. Please confirm.

The VQC is about 0.03 AUC behind the classical models at 12 features and about 0.07 behind at 24. At 8 features (8-qubit tier) it is about 0.01–0.02 below LR and 0.03–0.04 below RF.

8.7 Is it a model-size effect? Parameter-matched MLP

Shrinking the classical MLP to the VQC's size does not close the gap, and logistic regression with 13 parameters beats the 121-parameter VQC. We therefore make no parameter-efficiency claim.

9. Main observations

#Observation
1The data are very separable classically (AUC about 0.97 RF, 0.96 LR/MLP). A compact set of 32 features comes within 0.003–0.004 of the ceiling.
2Selection matters most when k is small: about +0.10 AUC over random for the VQC at k = 8.
3Under a fixed qubit budget, the tuned hybrid keeps the most information when features outnumber qubits (drop −0.04 vs −0.08 to −0.11 at 8 qubits; −0.025 vs −0.078 at 12 qubits).
4More qubits help; more layers do not.
5The circuit uses later-loaded features poorly (shuffle control).
6Mixing features (PCA/PLS) is worse than selecting real ECG features.
7Classical models stay ahead: about 0.03 AUC at 12 features and 0.07 at 24, and shrinking them does not close the gap.

10. Limitations and what is still to do

  • 5 folds and mostly one seed; the smallest possible sign-test p-value with 5 folds is 0.0625, so small differences cannot be called significant.
  • Hybrid weights were tuned at 8 features only (winner's curse is possible), and the hybrid's edge vanishes with 8 layers.
  • Exact simulation without hardware noise; fixed training hyperparameters (300 steps).
  • PTB-XL is single-source and MI vs normal is an easier problem than many clinical tasks. Features are hand-crafted ST/QRS/T measurements.
  • The official PTB-XL folds could not be used (no strat_fold in the metadata), so results are not directly comparable with published benchmarks.
  • To do: faster (adjoint) gradient for 16 qubits; layer-decay and input-scaling tests; a 3-round test at 8 qubits; swap-tails test; 3-seed main tier; robustness (imputation, noise, finite shots); re-check PCA/PLS numbers.

The PCA figures quoted in the abstract (36 components for 80% variance, silhouette 0.141, 20 features within the final 32) come from an earlier analysis and have not been re-checked in this report.
